q: What is the FIRST step you should take before beginning any data analysis?
options: Clearly define the business question the analysis is meant to answer
Build an initial chart so you can see the shape of the raw data
Import every available table into a spreadsheet so nothing is missed later
Remove duplicate records so the counts are accurate from the start
why: Defining the analysis objective ensures the work answers the right question before any data is touched.

q: A 'success criterion' in a data analysis project is best described as:
options: A measurable condition that confirms the objective has been met
The overall color scheme and layout of the final report
The total number of rows and columns contained in the dataset
The specific software tool chosen to perform the analysis
why: Success criteria set clear, measurable conditions that define when the objective has been achieved.

q: Which of the following is a well-scoped analysis objective?
options: Look at all of the sales data and see what stands out
Make the quarterly figures look clearer and more presentable
Determine which product category had the highest month-over-month growth in Q1
Find something interesting that leadership has not noticed yet
why: A good objective is specific, measurable, and tied to a concrete decision.

q: A Key Performance Indicator (KPI) is best defined as:
options: A standard chart format used for executive summary reporting
A specialized index used to speed up database table lookups
A measurable value showing how effectively an objective is being met
A raw, unprocessed value pulled directly from a source system
why: A KPI is a quantifiable metric used to gauge progress toward a defined goal.

q: Why is it important to identify stakeholders before starting an analysis?
options: To confirm that formulas will not be required for the final output
To deliberately increase the overall size and scope of the dataset
To justify taking additional time before delivering any findings
To understand who will use the results and what decisions they support
why: Knowing the audience shapes what questions to answer and how to present results.

q: 'Scope creep' during a data project refers to:
options: Source data gradually becoming corrupted over the project timeline
Records being deleted by accident during routine cleaning work
The objective expanding uncontrollably beyond the original question
A chart growing too large to fit within the report page
why: Scope creep is the uncontrolled expansion of a project's goals beyond what was originally agreed.

q: Which question best clarifies the analysis objective at the start of a project?
options: How many worksheet tabs will the finished workbook contain?
What naming convention should be used for the saved file?
Which typeface and heading style should the final report use?
What specific decision is this analysis intended to inform?
why: Tying analysis to a decision keeps the work focused and relevant.

q: A KPI differs from an ordinary metric in that a KPI is:
options: Always expressed as a percentage rather than a raw count
A value that, by definition, cannot be measured precisely
Identical to a metric, since the two terms mean the same thing
A metric tied directly to a specific strategic objective or goal
why: All KPIs are metrics, but only metrics tied directly to key objectives are KPIs.

q: Before analysis, defining the 'unit of analysis' means deciding:
options: Which measurement unit to use, such as meters, dollars, or hours
Which software license type is required for the analysis tool
What screen resolution the final dashboard should be built for
What each row in your dataset represents, e.g., a customer or an order
why: The unit of analysis defines what a single record represents, which shapes the entire dataset structure.

q: Which is an example of a 'leading' question that could bias an analysis objective?
options: Which region recorded the largest number of product returns?
How did total sales change over the past four fiscal quarters?
What underlying factors most influenced our recent customer churn?
Why is our product so clearly the best option on the market?
why: A leading question presumes a conclusion, biasing the analysis toward a predetermined answer.

q: Setting a clear objective at the outset helps prevent which common problem?
options: Saving the finished file in the wrong folder or format
Being required to use a spreadsheet instead of a database
Producing a bar chart when a line chart would be clearer
Spending effort analyzing data irrelevant to the actual decision
why: A clear objective keeps analysts from wasting effort on irrelevant data.

q: A well-formed 'business question' should ideally be:
options: Written only after the analysis has already been completed
Specific, answerable with data, and relevant to a real decision
Focused mainly on which tools and software will be used
Broad and open-ended so that almost any answer will satisfy it
why: Good business questions are specific, data-answerable, and decision-relevant.

q: When defining objectives, an 'actionable insight' means an insight that:
options: Leads directly to a concrete decision or a specific action
Looks impressive and polished when placed on a summary slide
Consists of a raw data export handed off to another team
Is simply any numeric value produced by a spreadsheet formula
why: Actionable insights drive real decisions rather than merely describing data.

q: A manager says only 'Sales seem off.' Which restatement best turns this into an objective?
options: Change the chart colors so the numbers are easier to read
Identify which regions and products declined versus the prior quarter
Add more rows of recent transactions to the existing report
Export the entire sales database and share it with the manager
why: Turning a vague concern into a specific, measurable question is the core of defining an objective.

q: In a well-structured (tidy) dataset, each column should represent:
options: A calculated formula applied to the surrounding data
A single variable or field measured across the observations
A finished chart summarizing the values in that section
A single complete record describing one observed entity
why: In tidy data, each column is one variable, each row is one observation.

q: In a tidy dataset, each row should represent:
options: A single observation or record, such as one customer or order
A single variable measured across every record in the table
A summary total aggregating the values in that column
A descriptive header labeling the fields shown below it
why: Each row is one observation; each column is one variable.

q: A CSV file stores tabular data by separating values with:
options: Tab characters placed between each field in a row
Semicolons that mark the end of every data column
Fixed-width spaces padding each field to equal length
Commas placed between each field value in a row
why: CSV stands for Comma-Separated Values.

q: Assigning the correct 'data type' to a column (e.g., date, number, text) matters because:
options: It has no real practical effect on how the data behaves
It changes the file extension used when the data is saved
It reduces the overall storage size taken up by the file
It determines how values can be sorted, calculated, and validated
why: Data types control valid operations, sorting behavior, and calculations.

q: A field storing the value '2026-08-27' should be assigned which data type for analysis?
options: Currency, so a monetary symbol is displayed alongside it
Text, so the exact characters are preserved as entered
Boolean, since the value resolves to either true or false
Date, so it can be sorted chronologically and used in calculations
why: Assigning a Date type enables chronological sorting and date calculations.

q: Which is a benefit of consistent field naming (e.g., 'first_name' rather than mixed styles)?
options: It serves a purely decorative role with no practical benefit
It changes the underlying values stored within each field
It reduces confusion and errors when referencing or joining data
It noticeably increases the physical size of the saved file
why: Consistent naming reduces reference errors, especially when joining datasets.

q: 'Structured data' is best described as data that:
options: Consists only of images, audio, and video file content
Cannot be opened or manipulated inside a spreadsheet
Has no predefined format and cannot be neatly organized
Is organized into rows and columns following a defined schema
why: Structured data follows a predefined model of rows, columns, and data types.

q: Which of the following is an example of UNstructured data?
options: A free-text customer review written in a support email
A comma-separated file exported from an ordering system
A normalized relational database table with defined keys
A spreadsheet listing monthly sales figures by region
why: Free-text has no predefined schema, making it unstructured.

q: A 'flat file' is best described as:
options: A damaged file that can no longer be opened correctly
A file that contains no usable data records at all
A file whose contents have been compressed to save space
A single table of data with no relationships to other tables
why: A flat file is a single, self-contained table without linked relationships.

q: When importing a CSV, the 'header row' typically contains:
options: A series of blank cells reserved for future entries
The column names or field labels for the data below
A totals row summarizing each column's numeric values
The very first complete data record in the dataset
why: The header row labels each column so fields can be identified.

q: In the context of importing data, a 'delimiter' is:
options: A password required before the file can be opened
The character used to separate fields, such as a comma or tab
A cap on the maximum file size that can be imported
A category of chart used to display the imported data
why: A delimiter marks the boundary between fields during import/parsing.

q: Storing a phone number as text rather than a number is often preferred because:
options: Text values always take up less storage space than numbers
Leading zeros and formatting like dashes are preserved as entered
It is a legal requirement in most data-handling standards
Numeric fields are technically unable to store any digits
why: Numeric types strip leading zeros and symbols; text preserves the exact format.

q: 'Wide' format data differs from 'long' format in that wide format:
options: Has one row per observation with variables spread across many columns
Cannot be analyzed until it is first converted to a database
Uses only a single column to store all of its values
Always contains more total rows than any other data arrangement
why: Wide data spreads variables across columns; long data stacks them into fewer columns with more rows.

q: Which practice improves the reliability of imported data?
options: Mixing several different data types within a single column
Merging every cell so the layout looks cleaner on screen
Verifying that each column holds a single, consistent data type
Removing all column headers before the analysis begins
why: Consistent data types per column prevent calculation and sorting errors.

q: A dataset's 'schema' describes:
options: A single representative value drawn from the dataset
The structure of the data: its fields, types, and organization
The category of chart chosen to present the results
The palette of colors used throughout the finished report
why: A schema defines the structure, fields, and data types of a dataset.

q: When a numeric column imports as text (e.g., '1,200' with a comma), the correct fix is to:
options: Convert them to a numeric type after removing the thousands separator
Delete the entire column and re-enter the figures manually
Leave the values unchanged, since they still appear correct
Rename the file so the import behaves differently next time
why: Converting to numeric enables calculations; the display separator must be handled during conversion.

q: 'Data cleaning' primarily aims to:
options: Encrypt the dataset so unauthorized users cannot read it
Improve data quality by fixing errors, inconsistencies, and gaps
Make the finished spreadsheet more colorful and visually appealing
Increase the total number of rows available for analysis
why: Cleaning improves accuracy and consistency before analysis.

q: Which of the following is a common data quality issue?
options: Category labels that follow a single, standardized naming style
Column totals that already reconcile with the source system
Duplicate records that appear more than once in the dataset
Dates that have been entered in a correct, consistent format
why: Duplicates are a frequent quality problem that distorts counts and sums.

q: Removing duplicate records is important because duplicates can:
options: Reduce the total storage size taken up by the file
Inflate counts and skew aggregated results such as sums
Improve the overall accuracy of the reported figures
Never cause any measurable problems in the analysis
why: Duplicates overstate counts and distort sums, averages, and other aggregates.

q: A 'null' or blank value in a dataset represents:
options: The specific numeric quantity of zero recorded on purpose
A short text label describing the adjacent data field
A negative number that fell below the allowed range
A missing or unknown value with no recorded content
why: Null indicates absence of a value, which is distinct from zero.

q: Why is a NULL different from a value of 0?
options: Zero is a known measured quantity, while NULL means the value is missing
Zero cannot be stored in a numeric field, but NULL can
They are effectively the same and can be used interchangeably
NULL is always treated as larger than zero in calculations
why: Zero is a real measured value; NULL means no value is recorded.

q: Which approach handles missing values by filling them with a substitute (like the column mean)?
options: Encryption, which scrambles the value so it is hidden
Imputation, which estimates and inserts a replacement value
Duplication, which copies a nearby record into the gap
Deletion, which removes the affected records entirely
why: Imputation replaces missing values with estimated substitutes.

q: 'Trimming' text data typically means:
options: Converting all of the text characters to uppercase
Translating the text into a different working language
Removing leading and trailing whitespace from the values
Deleting the column that contains the text values
why: Trimming removes extra spaces that cause mismatches and lookup failures.

q: Entries like 'NY', 'New York', and 'new york' for the same value should be:
options: Deleted entirely so the inconsistency cannot cause errors
Left exactly as they are to preserve the original entry
Standardized to a single consistent form before grouping
Converted into numeric codes with no lookup reference
why: Standardizing categorical values ensures accurate grouping and counts.

q: An 'outlier' is best described as:
options: A label placed at the top of a column to name the field
A blank cell where no value was ever recorded at all
The single most frequently occurring value in the dataset
A value that falls far outside the typical range of the data
why: An outlier lies well outside the normal distribution of values.

q: Before removing an outlier, an analyst should FIRST:
options: Discard the whole dataset and request a fresh export
Investigate whether it is a data error or a genuine extreme value
Duplicate it so the unusual pattern is preserved for review
Delete it right away so it cannot distort the results
why: Outliers may be legitimate; they should be understood before removal.

q: 'Data transformation' includes which of the following activities?
options: Only deleting rows that contain one or more empty cells
Converting units, aggregating, or reshaping data into a usable form
Only renaming the file after the analysis is complete
Only changing the fill colors applied to certain cells
why: Transformation reshapes or converts data into a form suitable for analysis.

q: Standardizing date formats across a column (e.g., all as YYYY-MM-DD) helps to:
options: Enable correct chronological sorting and reliable date calculations
Corrupt the underlying values so they can no longer be read
Hide the dates from anyone viewing the finished report
Increase the ambiguity of when each event actually occurred
why: A consistent date format allows chronological sorting and accurate date math.

q: 'Normalization' of data values (e.g., scaling to a 0–1 range) is used to:
options: Bring variables measured on different scales onto a comparable one
Delete outliers automatically without any prior investigation
Add duplicate rows to increase the size of the dataset
Encrypt the values so they cannot be read without a key
why: Scaling normalization puts variables on a comparable range for fair comparison.

q: Which of the following is an example of a data 'consistency' error?
options: A customer's country stored as 'USA' in one row and 'United States' in another
A unique identifier that appears exactly once across the dataset
A date value that has been entered in the standard expected format
A person's name that has been spelled correctly throughout the file
why: Consistency errors are the same concept represented in conflicting ways.

q: 'Data validation' rules (e.g., age must fall between 0 and 120) help by:
options: Slowing down the pace at which data can be entered
Preventing invalid or impossible values from entering the dataset
Deleting values that are already known to be correct
Changing the fonts applied to the affected cells
why: Validation rules block impossible or out-of-range entries at the source.

q: Converting a 'Full Name' column into separate 'First Name' and 'Last Name' columns is:
options: A deletion step that discards part of the recorded information
A duplication step that copies the name into a new column
A form of encryption that conceals the original name values
An example of splitting or parsing one field into several fields
why: Splitting parses one field into multiple structured fields.

q: Which is a valid reason to DELETE rows with missing values rather than impute them?
options: Deleting rows is never acceptable under any circumstances
When the missing values are few and unlikely to bias the results
When the affected column is the most important in the dataset
When you intend to fabricate plausible-looking replacement data
why: Row deletion is acceptable when missing data is minimal and non-systematic.

q: 'Deduplication' requires identifying a record as a duplicate based on:
options: The position of the row relative to the others in the file
One or more key fields that uniquely identify each record
The type of chart selected to display the final results
The background fill color applied to the record's cells
why: Duplicates are detected by comparing key identifying fields.

q: A 'data type mismatch' error occurs when:
options: The file has just been saved to disk without any content being changed
Every value in a column already shares the same expected data type
Cell color formatting has been applied across a wide range of cells
A value's type conflicts with the column's expected type, e.g., text in a numeric field
why: Mismatches happen when a value doesn't match the column's defined type.

q: Changing all text in a column to lowercase before matching is done to:
options: Make the finished report look more visually appealing
Increase the overall storage size taken up by the file
Ensure that case differences do not cause false mismatches
Delete records whose text does not meet a condition
why: Case-folding prevents 'Apple' and 'apple' from being treated as different.

q: Which best describes 'aggregation' as a data transformation?
options: Scrambling field values so they cannot be read directly
Splitting one populated column into several separate columns
Combining many detailed records into summary values like sums or averages
Removing duplicate records that appear more than once
why: Aggregation rolls detailed records up into summary statistics.

q: An entry of '999' used to mean 'no answer' in a survey age field is problematic because:
options: It is guaranteed to always be the correct recorded value
It represents a completely valid and ordinary recorded age
It is a placeholder that distorts calculations if treated as real
It cannot physically be stored inside a numeric field
why: Sentinel/placeholder codes distort averages and totals if not handled as missing.

q: A 'lookup' function is used to:
options: Retrieve a related value from another table using a matching key
Change the fill colors applied throughout an entire chart area
Permanently delete the rows that meet a specified matching condition
Sort the values contained within a single selected column
why: Lookups fetch related values by matching a key across tables.

q: To combine two datasets by matching records, they must share:
options: A common key, that is, a matching field to join on
The same set of fill colors applied to their cells
An identical file name saved in the same folder
Exactly the same number of columns in each table
why: A common key links records across datasets.

q: A 'primary key' in a table is:
options: A formula that recalculates whenever the data changes
A field that uniquely identifies each record in the table
A password that must be entered to open the table
Always the first column, regardless of its contents
why: A primary key uniquely identifies every row in a table.

q: A 'foreign key' is:
options: A duplicate copy of a primary key stored for backup
A field that references the primary key of another table
An identifier assigned to records originating in another country
An encrypted value used to secure the record's contents
why: A foreign key links to another table's primary key, forming a relationship.

q: An 'inner join' returns:
options: Only the rows that have matching keys in both tables
Only the rows that fail to match in either table
Every possible combination of rows from both tables
Every row from both tables regardless of any matches
why: An inner join keeps only records with matches in both tables.

q: A 'left join' returns:
options: All rows from the left table plus matching rows from the right
Only the rows drawn from the right table in the join
Only the rows that successfully match in both tables
No rows at all unless every key matches perfectly
why: A left join keeps all left-table rows, filling unmatched right values with nulls.

q: If a lookup returns an error or a blank for a value, a likely cause is:
options: Too many distinct fill colors have been applied to the source cells
The overall file is far too small for the program to process it
A required chart has been left out of the current workbook
The key value is missing from the lookup table or has extra spaces
why: Lookup failures usually stem from missing keys or whitespace/format mismatches.

q: 'Concatenation' of data means:
options: Joining text values from multiple fields into one
Deleting fields that are no longer needed for analysis
Splitting a single populated field into several fields
Encrypting text so it cannot be read without a key
why: Concatenation combines multiple text values into a single string.

q: When combining datasets, mismatched key formats (e.g., 'ID001' vs '1') will cause:
options: Perfectly reliable matches between every pair of records
No effect whatsoever on how the records are joined
Noticeably faster processing of the combined result
Failed or incorrect matches between the two datasets
why: Keys must be in a consistent format to match correctly.

q: A 'one-to-many' relationship exists when:
options: Every record matches exactly one record in the other table
One record in Table A relates to many records in Table B
There are no defined relationships between the two tables
The two tables are exact duplicates of one another
why: One customer relating to many orders is a classic one-to-many relationship.

q: Appending (stacking) two datasets vertically requires that they:
options: Have all of their header rows removed beforehand
Be saved in two different file formats before merging
Share the same columns and overall structure
Contain completely different sets of columns and fields
why: Appending stacks rows, so the column structures must align.

q: The main risk of joining on a non-unique key is:
options: The result will end up with fewer columns than intended
Unintended row multiplication, a 'fan-out' of duplicated records
The join will complete noticeably faster than expected
There is no real risk associated with this kind of join
why: Joining on non-unique keys can multiply rows unexpectedly and distort totals.

q: An 'approximate match' lookup is most appropriate for:
options: Matching exact customer identifiers between two systems
Matching email addresses that must agree character for character
Matching product SKUs that must be identical to be valid
Placing a value into a range or bracket, such as tax brackets
why: Approximate match suits range-based lookups like grading or tax brackets.

q: Before joining two tables, verifying key uniqueness helps prevent:
options: Duplicate or inflated rows from appearing in the output
Proper formatting from being applied to the final table
Faster completion of the overall analysis process
Correct, expected results appearing in the joined output
why: Checking key uniqueness avoids accidental record multiplication.

q: The 'mean' of a dataset is:
options: The value that occurs most frequently across the data
The middle value once all the numbers are sorted in order
The difference between the largest and smallest values
The sum of all the values divided by how many there are
why: The mean is the arithmetic average.

q: The 'median' is:
options: The average obtained by summing and dividing all values
The middle value once the data has been sorted in order
The value that appears most often in the dataset
The gap between the maximum and minimum values
why: The median is the central value in an ordered dataset.

q: The 'mode' is:
options: The value that occurs most frequently in the dataset
The average calculated across all values in the set
The middle value found once the data is sorted
The difference between the highest and lowest values
why: The mode is the value that appears most often.

q: When a dataset contains extreme outliers, which measure of central tendency is LEAST affected?
options: The total, because it reflects the full magnitude of the data
The median, because it depends only on the middle position
The mean, because it incorporates every single value
The sum, because it adds together all of the values
why: The median is resistant to outliers, unlike the mean.

q: 'Range' as a measure of spread is calculated as:
options: The maximum value minus the minimum value in the data
The middle value once the numbers have been sorted
The count of how many values appear in the dataset
The average of all values across the entire dataset
why: Range is the difference between the maximum and minimum.

q: 'Standard deviation' measures:
options: The single value that appears most often in the data
The number of records contained in the dataset
How spread out the values are around the mean
The typical average value across the whole dataset
why: Standard deviation quantifies dispersion around the mean.

q: A value increasing from 200 to 250 represents a percentage change of:
options: A 20% increase relative to the new value
A 25% increase relative to the original value
A 5% increase across the two figures
A change of 50 measured in absolute units

q: 'Correlation' describes:
options: A guarantee that one variable directly causes the other
The strength and direction of a relationship between two variables
A row that has been duplicated within the dataset
A record whose value is missing from the dataset
why: Correlation measures how two variables move together, not causation.

q: The principle 'correlation does not imply causation' means:
options: Two variables that move together always cause each other
Causation between any two variables is effectively impossible
A relationship between variables does not prove one causes the other
Correlation is meaningless and should never be measured
why: Variables can correlate without a direct causal link, possibly via a third factor.

q: A 'trend' in time-series data refers to:
options: The general direction in which values move over time
A descriptive label placed at the top of a column
A duplicate row mistakenly included in the dataset
A single isolated data point at one moment in time
why: A trend is the overall long-term direction of the data over time.

q: A 'moving average' is used to:
options: Permanently delete older data from the series
Introduce additional outliers into the dataset
Encrypt the values so they cannot be read directly
Smooth out short-term fluctuations to reveal a trend
why: Moving averages smooth noise to highlight the underlying trend.

q: Which spreadsheet function computes the total of a range of cells?
options: LEN, which reports the length of a text string
MAX, which returns the single largest value present
COUNT, which tallies how many numeric entries exist
SUM, which adds together all the values in the range
why: SUM totals the values in a range.

q: The COUNT function returns:
options: The combined total of all the values in a range
The average of all the values within the range
The single largest value found within the range
The number of numeric entries contained in a range
why: COUNT tallies how many numeric values are present.

q: A conditional function such as COUNTIF is used to:
options: Count only the cells that meet a specified condition
Sort the cells into ascending or descending order
Count every cell in the range without exception
Delete the cells that do not meet a condition
why: COUNTIF counts only entries that satisfy a given criterion.

q: A 'weighted average' differs from a simple average in that it:
options: Cannot be calculated using standard spreadsheet formulas
Is always numerically smaller than a simple average
Gives some values more influence based on assigned weights
Ignores most of the values when producing a result
why: Weighted averages account for the relative importance of each value.

q: 'Descriptive statistics' primarily aim to:
options: Summarize and describe the main features of a dataset
Predict future outcomes based on the observed data
Encrypt the dataset so it is protected from access
Join two separate tables into one combined dataset
why: Descriptive statistics summarize what the data shows.

q: For the values 10, 12, 12, and 100, the MEAN is most heavily influenced by:
options: The value 10, which is the smallest in the set
The value 12, which appears twice in the set
The value 100, which is the outlier in the set
The value 0, which is not present in the set
why: The outlier 100 pulls the mean upward, illustrating outlier sensitivity.

q: Month-over-month 'rate of growth' is best expressed as:
options: A single raw total covering the entire period
A percentage change between two consecutive months
The physical file size of the monthly data export
A plain count of the records added each month
why: Growth rate is a percentage change between periods.

q: Which chart type is BEST for showing a trend over time?
options: A word cloud sizing terms by how often they appear
A line chart plotting values across a continuous time axis
A pie chart dividing the total into proportional slices
A single-value card displaying one summary number
why: Line charts excel at showing change over continuous time.

q: A 'bar chart' is most appropriate for:
options: Comparing values across distinct, separate categories
Showing the parts that make up a single whole
Showing correlation between two continuous variables
Displaying just one summary number on its own
why: Bar charts compare discrete categories effectively.

q: A 'pie chart' is best used to show:
options: A dense time series with many closely spaced points
The correlation between two continuous measurements
Parts of a whole, or proportions, for a few categories
A detailed trend measured across many years
why: Pie charts show composition, but only work well with a few categories.

q: A 'scatter plot' is best suited to reveal:
options: The count of records that fall into each category
The relationship or correlation between two numeric variables
A single aggregated total for the whole dataset
A ranked list ordering items from highest to lowest
why: Scatter plots visualize the relationship between two continuous variables.

q: A common way to MISLEAD a reader with a bar chart is to:
options: Sort the bars so they read from largest to smallest
Clearly label both axes with their units and scale
Start the y-axis at a value other than zero to exaggerate differences
Give the chart a clear and descriptive title
why: A truncated y-axis visually exaggerates small differences.

q: A 'pivot table' is used to:
options: Encrypt the underlying data so it cannot be read
Draw a scatter plot of two continuous variables
Summarize and aggregate data by grouping selected fields
Delete duplicate records from the source dataset
why: Pivot tables quickly aggregate and cross-tabulate data.

q: The MAIN purpose of a data visualization is to:
options: Conceal the underlying data from the audience
Communicate insights clearly and support decisions
Increase the overall file size of the deliverable
Decorate the report so it looks more professional
why: Visualizations should clarify the message and aid decisions.

q: A 'dashboard' typically provides:
options: A single raw data table with no summarization
An encrypted file that requires a key to open
A long written list of the formulas that were used
An at-a-glance view of key metrics and visualizations
why: Dashboards consolidate key metrics into an at-a-glance view.

q: When choosing a chart, the FIRST consideration should be:
options: Which file format the finished chart will be saved in
Which combination of colors looks the most attractive
Which font size will fill the available space best
The message or question the chart is meant to answer
why: Chart choice should follow from the insight you need to communicate.

q: Which of the following is a best practice for clear visualizations?
options: Apply 3D effects to every chart for visual interest
Label the axes, add a descriptive title, and avoid clutter
Remove all labels so the chart looks cleaner
Use many colors that carry no particular meaning
why: Clear labels, honest scales, and minimal clutter improve comprehension.

domain: 7. Data Integrity, Ethics, and Sharing Results
q: 'Data integrity' refers to:
options: The palette of colors used across the charts
The total number of tables contained in the database
The accuracy, consistency, and reliability of data over its lifecycle
The physical file size of the stored dataset
why: Data integrity is the maintenance of accuracy and consistency throughout the data's life.

domain: 7. Data Integrity, Ethics, and Sharing Results
q: Personally Identifiable Information (PII) includes:
options: Data that can identify an individual, such as a name, email, or ID
Aggregated totals that cannot be traced back to any one person
The descriptive header labels placed at the top of each column
The colors that were chosen for a particular chart or dashboard
why: PII is any data that can identify a specific person and must be protected.

domain: 7. Data Integrity, Ethics, and Sharing Results
q: A key ethical practice when sharing analysis results is to:
options: Present results honestly, including limitations and uncertainty
Fabricate supporting figures to strengthen the conclusion
Remove all references to where the data originated
Conceal any findings that reflect poorly on the outcome
why: Ethical reporting requires transparency about limitations and honesty in findings.

domain: 7. Data Integrity, Ethics, and Sharing Results
q: 'Anonymization' of data is performed to:
options: Increase the overall storage size of the file
Introduce additional duplicate records into the data
Make the dataset impossible to analyze in any way
Protect individual privacy by removing or masking identifying details
why: Anonymization protects privacy by stripping identifying information.

domain: 7. Data Integrity, Ethics, and Sharing Results
q: 'Cherry-picking' data is an ethical violation because it:
options: Makes use of all of the available evidence fairly
Selectively presents only the data that supports a desired conclusion
Improves the overall accuracy of the reported results
Removes duplicate records before the analysis begins
why: Cherry-picking presents a biased subset to mislead, misrepresenting reality.

domain: 7. Data Integrity, Ethics, and Sharing Results
q: Before sharing a report widely, an analyst should verify:
options: Only that the chosen color scheme looks consistent from slide to slide
The accuracy of the data, appropriate access permissions, and protection of sensitive info
Nothing in particular, since sharing a finished report carries no real risk
Only that the saved file has been given an appropriate descriptive name
why: Responsible sharing checks accuracy, access control, and protection of sensitive data.

q: A marketing manager tells you, 'Our campaign isn't working — figure out why.' Before pulling any data, what is your BEST next step?
options: Assume the underlying concern is click-through rate and quietly proceed with that metric
Build a polished dashboard right away so the manager has something concrete to review
Export every campaign table you can find and immediately start exploring the raw numbers
Ask what 'working' means and which metric defines success, such as conversions or ROI
why: A vague request must be translated into a specific, measurable objective by clarifying the success metric before analysis begins.

q: Your dean asks for 'a report on student performance.' Which clarifying question BEST scopes the objective?
options: What color scheme and visual theme should be applied across the charts in the report?
Which cohort, subject, and time period should the report cover, and what decision will it support?
Roughly how many pages long should the finished report be when it is submitted?
Which font family would you prefer to see used for the headings and the body text?
why: Scoping requires nailing down population, timeframe, and the decision the report informs.

q: A stakeholder keeps adding new questions mid-project: 'Also add region, and gender, and last year too.' This situation is an example of:
options: A routine data-cleaning task that is expected during any project
Sound objective-setting done collaboratively with the stakeholder
A join error that appeared when combining the source tables
Scope creep that should be documented and re-negotiated with the stakeholder
why: Uncontrolled expansion of the request beyond the agreed objective is scope creep.

q: You are asked to 'prove that our new product is the best.' Why is this objective problematic?
options: It is a leading objective that presumes its conclusion and invites biased analysis
It describes a goal that simply cannot be measured with data
It is far too narrow and specific to produce any useful result
It is perfectly neutral and does not steer the analysis at all
why: An objective that assumes its own conclusion biases the entire analysis.

q: An operations lead wants to reduce delivery delays but hasn't defined a target. What should you establish FIRST?
options: The overall color theme that the final delivery-tracking dashboard should follow
The total number of individual delivery records that the source dataset contains
A measurable success criterion, e.g., cutting average delay from three days to under one
Which chart type will best display the delivery delay figures once they are ready
why: A measurable success criterion turns a goal into something the analysis can actually evaluate.

q: Two departments define 'active user' differently. Before analyzing 'active users,' you should:
options: Quietly pick one of the two definitions and proceed without noting it
Report both figures side by side without flagging that they differ
Ignore the discrepancy since the two definitions are probably close
Agree on a single shared definition of the metric with the stakeholders
why: Ambiguous metric definitions must be reconciled up front to avoid inconsistent results.

q: You import a CSV and a column of order totals shows as left-aligned text like '1,250.00'. What is the MOST likely issue and fix?
options: Nothing is wrong, since the values still display in a readable form
The whole file is corrupt and should be downloaded again from the source
The column imported as text; convert it to numeric after handling the thousands separator
The column serves no purpose and can simply be deleted from the sheet
why: Left-aligned numbers usually signal a text import; converting to numeric enables calculations.

q: A dataset has one row per customer with 12 separate columns Jan_Sales through Dec_Sales. To analyze monthly trends easily, you should:
options: Reshape it from wide to long, with a Month column and a Sales column
Leave it in wide form and hope the analysis still works out
Merge all twelve monthly columns into a single combined cell
Delete eleven of the columns and keep only the most recent month
why: Converting wide to long (one row per month) makes time-series analysis and charting far easier.

q: A ZIP or postal code column contains values like 01234 but they appear as 1234 after import. The correct handling is to:
options: Delete the rows whose codes lost a leading zero during import
Store the field as text so the leading zeros are preserved as entered
Multiply every value in the column by ten to restore the digits
Accept the loss of the leading zero as an unavoidable outcome
why: Numeric types strip leading zeros; postal codes should be stored as text.

q: You receive data where each row mixes a customer AND their most recent order in one record, making the unit of analysis unclear. This is a problem because:
options: It is ambiguous whether a row represents a customer or an order, which distorts counts
It noticeably reduces the overall storage size that the dataset takes up on disk
It improves the accuracy of any totals or averages calculated from the data
It is actually the ideal structure for nearly any analysis you might run
why: A dataset must have a clear, consistent unit of analysis for counts and aggregates to be valid.

q: A colleague sends a spreadsheet with merged cells spanning several header columns. Before analysis you should:
options: Convert the entire spreadsheet into a static image so the layout is preserved
Analyze the file exactly as it was received without altering any of the headers
Add several more merged cells so that the header layout looks a little tidier
Unmerge the cells and build a single clean header row so the fields parse correctly
why: Merged header cells break structured parsing; a single clean header row is required.

q: A date column mixes formats: '08/27/2026', '2026-08-27', and 'Aug 27, 2026'. The BEST structuring step is to:
options: Leave the formats mixed, since all three clearly still refer to real dates
Delete the entire column because the inconsistent formats make it unusable
Convert all of the varied dates into plain text values and simply stop there
Standardize every value to one date format and set the column's type to Date
why: A single consistent date type enables correct sorting and date calculations.

q: You must combine sales files from three regions that use different column orders but the same fields. Before appending them you should:
options: Randomize the row order within each of the files before combining them together
Delete the smallest of the three regional files in order to simplify the overall merge
Stack the three files in whatever order they each happen to arrive in from the regions
Align the columns and field names so that the same data lands in the same column
why: Appending requires matching column structures so values align correctly.

q: A customer list shows the same person twice: 'Juan Dela Cruz' and ' Juan Dela Cruz' (leading space), inflating your counts. The fix is to:
options: Add a third identical copy so the count is at least consistent
Keep both entries so no potential customer is ever lost
Trim the whitespace first, then deduplicate on the cleaned key
Delete the customer entirely to avoid any double counting
why: Trimming whitespace first ensures the two entries match so deduplication works.

q: A 'Country' field contains 'PH', 'Philippines', and 'philippines' for the same country, splitting your group totals. You should:
options: Standardize all of the variants to one consistent value before grouping
Report the three spellings as if they were three separate countries
Delete the entire country field so the inconsistency disappears
Convert the country names into arbitrary numeric codes instead
why: Standardizing categorical variants ensures accurate grouping and counts.

q: An 'Age' column contains a value of 999, which is a survey placeholder for 'no answer.' If left in, it will:
options: Actually improve the overall accuracy of the reported average age across respondents
Have no measurable effect whatsoever on any statistic that you happen to calculate
Be recognized as a placeholder and then ignored automatically by the spreadsheet program
Distort the mean and other statistics, so it must be treated as a missing value
why: Sentinel placeholder codes must be converted to NULL, or they corrupt statistics.

q: A sales column has three blank cells out of 5,000 rows. Removing those rows is reasonable because:
options: Missing data should never be filled in through imputation methods
The missing values are minimal and unlikely to bias the overall results
Rows containing any blank cell cannot be analyzed under any method
Blank cells should always be interpreted as a recorded zero
why: When missing data is minimal and non-systematic, row deletion is a defensible choice.

q: You spot one transaction of ₱9,000,000 in a dataset where all others fall under ₱10,000. Before removing it you should:
options: Delete the record immediately so it cannot skew the totals
Duplicate the record so the unusual pattern is clearly preserved
Investigate whether it is a data-entry error or a legitimate large sale
Discard the whole dataset and request a completely fresh export
why: Outliers may be genuine; investigate the cause before deciding to remove.

q: Two columns store price as '₱1,200' stored as text and you need to sum them. The transformation required is to:
options: Strip the currency symbol and separators, convert to numeric, then sum
Concatenate the two text values into one longer string
Sort the price column before attempting the calculation
Change the font of the price cells to a numeric-looking style
why: Text-formatted currency must be converted to numeric before arithmetic.

q: A lookup keeps failing on email addresses. You find some are 'USER@MAIL.COM' and others 'user@mail.com'. The cleaning step is to:
options: Add extra spaces around the addresses to force them to align
Delete every row whose email case does not already match
Leave the mixed capitalization exactly as it was received
Standardize the case, e.g., lowercase, on both sides before matching
why: Case-folding both sides prevents case differences from causing false mismatches.

q: A 'Full Name' column must feed a mail-merge that greets people by first name only. The needed transformation is to:
options: Merge the name column together with the mailing address field
Delete the name column since it is not needed for the merge
Split or parse the name into separate First and Last name fields
Encrypt the name column so the values are protected in transit
why: Parsing one field into structured parts enables first-name personalization.

q: You need to compare exam scores (0–100) with attendance (0–30 days) in one model, but their scales differ wildly. A reasonable transformation is to:
options: Leave the two variables incomparable and analyze them separately
Add the two raw values together to create one combined figure
Delete one of the two variables so only a single scale remains
Normalize or scale both variables onto a common comparable range
why: Scaling variables to a comparable range allows fair comparison across different units.

q: An entry-error check reveals a 'quantity' field with a negative value of -5 for items sold. The BEST action is to:
options: Silently multiply it by negative one and move on without a note
Delete the entire table because one value is clearly wrong
Keep the negative value, treating it as a valid quantity sold
Flag it as an invalid value and investigate or correct the entry
why: Impossible values should be flagged and investigated; silent changes hide data-quality issues.

q: You join a Customers table to an Orders table on CustomerID and the row count unexpectedly triples. The MOST likely cause is:
options: Neither of the two tables actually contains any key column
The join type used was an inner join rather than a left join
CustomerID is not unique in one table, so matching rows multiply
The chart built from the result was configured incorrectly
why: Joining on a non-unique key fans out rows, inflating the result set.

q: A VLOOKUP returns #N/A for several product IDs that you know exist. The MOST likely reason is:
options: A required chart is missing from the worksheet holding the data
Trailing spaces or format differences in the key block an exact match
The lookup formula itself is fundamentally impossible to write
The workbook file is simply far too large to process correctly
why: Whitespace or format mismatches in the lookup key are a classic cause of failed matches.

q: You need every customer to appear in a report even if they have no orders yet. The correct join is:
options: No join at all, working from the customer table on its own
A left join keeping all customers and their orders where they exist
An inner join returning only customers who placed an order
A join deliberately configured to drop customers without orders
why: A left join preserves all customers, filling missing order data with nulls.

q: You only want customers who actually placed at least one order. The correct join is:
options: No join at all, since the orders table already lists customers
An inner join returning only records that match in both tables
A full outer join that combines all rows from both tables
A left join that keeps every customer in the final result
why: An inner join returns only records that match in both tables.

q: Two systems store CustomerID as 'C001' in one and '1' in the other. Before joining you must:
options: Delete one of the two tables to avoid the formatting conflict
Sort both tables by CustomerID before running the join
Join the two tables as they are and accept the mismatches
Standardize the key format so the values in each table actually match
why: Keys must share a consistent format to match across tables.

q: You want to bucket exam scores into letter grades (90–100 = A, 80–89 = B, and so on). The appropriate lookup style is:
options: An inner join performed on the students' full names
A concatenation that joins the score and the letter together
An approximate or range match against a grade-bracket table
An exact match against a table of every possible score
why: Range-based classification (grades, tax brackets) calls for an approximate/range lookup.

q: After a join, totals are far higher than the source system reports. Your FIRST diagnostic check should be:
options: Delete the report and rebuild it from scratch without checking
Verify key uniqueness and whether the join multiplied the rows
Switch the chart type to see whether the totals then look right
Apply additional colors to the table to make it easier to read
why: Inflated post-join totals usually trace to non-unique keys causing row multiplication.

q: You must enrich an orders file with product prices from a separate catalog. The right technique is to:
options: Estimate each price by guessing based on the product name
Retype the correct price manually into every single order row
Use a lookup keyed on ProductID to pull prices from the catalog
Delete the price column entirely since it is stored elsewhere
why: A lookup on a shared key efficiently pulls related values from another table.

q: You are appending this quarter's sales to last quarter's file, but this quarter added a new 'DiscountCode' column. Before appending you should decide:
options: To randomize the column order in both files before merging
How to reconcile the extra column so the two structures align
To delete this quarter's data because its columns do not match
Nothing at all; simply stack the two files on top of each other
why: Appending requires aligned structures; the mismatched column must be reconciled first.

q: Employee salaries are ₱20k, ₱22k, ₱23k, and ₱500k (the CEO). To describe a 'typical' salary, which measure is most appropriate?
options: The median, because it resists the influence of the extreme outlier
The maximum, because it reflects the top of the pay scale
The range, because it captures the full spread of the salaries
The mean, because it makes use of every value in the set
why: With a strong outlier, the median better represents the typical value than the mean.

q: Monthly revenue jumps around a lot week to week, hiding the overall direction. To reveal the underlying trend you would apply:
options: A moving average that smooths the short-term fluctuations
A deduplication pass to remove repeated revenue records
An inner join between the revenue and calendar tables
A pie chart breaking revenue into proportional weekly slices
why: Moving averages smooth noise to expose the underlying trend.

q: Sales rose from ₱200,000 to ₱250,000. The percentage increase is:
options: A 20% increase relative to the original sales figure
A 25% increase relative to the original sales figure
A 50% increase relative to the original sales figure
A 5% increase relative to the original sales figure

q: You find that ice-cream sales and drowning incidents both rise in the same months and strongly correlate. The correct interpretation is:
options: Buying more ice cream is directly causing more drownings
The data must be wrong because the two cannot be related
The rise in drownings is what causes ice-cream sales to increase
Correlation does not imply causation; a third factor like hot weather drives both
why: Correlated variables may share a common cause rather than causing each other.

q: You must report how many students scored above 75. The most direct spreadsheet function is:
options: LEN, measuring the length of each score's text value
MAX, returning the single highest score in the column
SUM, adding together all of the scores in the column
COUNTIF, counting the entries that satisfy the condition '>75'
why: COUNTIF counts only entries meeting the specified condition.

q: A course grade weights the final exam at 50% and two quizzes at 25% each. Computing the grade requires a:
options: Median that reports the middle of the three scores
Weighted average that reflects each component's assigned weight
Simple average that treats every component equally
Mode that reports whichever score occurs most often
why: When components carry different weights, a weighted average is required.

q: Two datasets share the same mean, but one has a much larger standard deviation. This tells you that dataset:
options: Is guaranteed to contain no outliers of any kind
Is essentially identical to the other in every respect
Has values that are more spread out around the mean
Contains noticeably fewer records than the other dataset
why: A larger standard deviation indicates greater dispersion around the mean.

q: You want to summarize a dataset's central tendency and spread before deciding on next steps. You are applying:
options: Inferential statistics used to predict beyond the sample
Data encryption used to protect the values from access
A left join used to combine two related tables
Descriptive statistics used to summarize the dataset's features
why: Summarizing the main features of a dataset is descriptive statistics.

q: You must show how monthly website traffic changed across 24 months. The BEST chart is a:
options: Single-value card showing the total traffic across all months
Scatter plot of the month names against one another
Pie chart dividing total traffic into monthly proportional slices
Line chart plotting traffic across the continuous 24-month axis
why: Line charts are ideal for showing change over continuous time.

q: You want to compare total sales across six product categories for a single month. The BEST chart is a:
options: Scatter plot relating category names to one another
3D exploded pie chart with a separate slice per category
Line chart plotting a single month as one connected point
Bar chart comparing the six categories side by side
why: Bar charts compare values across discrete categories clearly.

q: A colleague's bar chart makes a 2% difference look enormous. You notice the y-axis starts at 95 instead of 0. This is:
options: A routine data-cleaning step performed before charting
A misleading truncated axis that visually exaggerates the difference
A recognized best practice for drawing clear bar charts
A necessary requirement whenever bar charts are created
why: A truncated y-axis visually overstates small differences and misleads readers.

q: You need to explore whether study hours relate to exam scores across 200 students. The BEST visualization is a:
options: Pie chart dividing the students into proportional score bands
Word cloud sizing student names by how often they appear
Scatter plot of study hours against exam scores per student
Single bar summarizing the average score for all students
why: Scatter plots reveal the relationship between two continuous variables.

q: An executive wants an at-a-glance view of five key metrics that is updated regularly. You should build a:
options: Single pie chart attempting to show all five metrics at once
Dashboard consolidating the five key metrics and their visuals
Long written paragraph describing each metric in full detail
Raw data dump containing every underlying transaction row
why: Dashboards present key metrics at a glance for quick decision-making.

q: You have detailed transaction rows and need sales summarized by region and month quickly. The most efficient tool is a:
options: Word cloud sizing region names by their sales volume
Pivot table that groups and aggregates the data by region and month
A single formula placed in one cell of the worksheet
Scatter plot relating each transaction to the next one
why: Pivot tables rapidly group and aggregate detailed data into summaries.

domain: 7. Data Integrity, Ethics, and Sharing Results
q: You are about to email a spreadsheet containing customer names, emails, and ID numbers to an external vendor. Before sending you should:
options: Mask or remove PII the vendor does not need and verify access permissions
Add several more personal fields so the vendor has full context
Post the file to a public location so it is easy for them to reach
Send the file as-is quickly so the vendor is not kept waiting
why: Responsible sharing means minimizing and protecting PII and controlling access.

domain: 7. Data Integrity, Ethics, and Sharing Results
q: Your analysis shows the campaign underperformed, but your manager asks you to 'only show the good weeks.' The ethical response is to:
options: Present only the good weeks exactly as the manager requested
Present the complete, honest results including the underperformance and its limitations
Fabricate stronger numbers so the campaign appears successful
Permanently delete the underperforming weeks from the dataset
why: Selectively showing only favorable data is cherry-picking, an ethical violation.

domain: 7. Data Integrity, Ethics, and Sharing Results
q: You want to share aggregated regional trends from a health dataset without exposing individuals. You should:
options: Publish the raw individual patient records for full transparency
Add patient names to the summary so the trends are easier to read
Anonymize the data by removing or masking identifying details before sharing
Email the complete unmodified dataset directly to the recipients
why: Anonymization protects privacy while still allowing aggregate insights to be shared.

domain: 7. Data Integrity, Ethics, and Sharing Results
q: After finishing a report, you realize one source table was last updated two years ago. The responsible action is to:
options: Hide the report so no one notices the outdated information
Manually change the dates so the source appears more recent
Verify the data's currency and disclose the limitation, or refresh the source
Publish the report without any comment about the stale source
why: Data integrity requires verifying accuracy and being transparent about limitations.
